title: Did globalisation cause the First World War?
gist: Reviewing William Mulligan's The Fraying Bonds of Peace, the piece argues that the first age of globalisation before 1914 did not guarantee peace: deep economic interdependence created both restraints and vulnerabilities, and as states militarised their foreign policy to counter those vulnerabilities, trade links became a source of conflict rather than a barrier to it.

themes.theme: Interdependence is not a peace guarantee

insights.claim: Deep economic interdependence generates vulnerabilities as well as benefits, and when states militarise their foreign policy to counter those vulnerabilities, trade links become a source of conflict rather than a guarantor of peace.
insights.speaker: Duncan Weldon
insights.so_what: Directly relevant to today's decoupling debates: economic integration cuts both ways, so investors should not assume trade ties alone will restrain great-power conflict.
insights.quote: Deeper trading and financial links can just as easily become a source of tension as a guarantor of peace.

insights.claim: The structure of the global economy is interlinked with the geopolitical order, so changes in one spill directly into the other.
insights.speaker: Duncan Weldon
insights.so_what: A framing for treating macroeconomic and geopolitical risk as a single coupled system rather than separate silos.
insights.quote: The nature and structure of the global economy is interlinked with the geopolitical order and changes in one can easily spill over into the other.

themes.theme: The first age of globalisation, quantified

insights.claim: Economic historians see the decades before 1914 as the first great age of globalisation, when measures of global economic integration hit levels not surpassed again in many cases until the 1980s.
insights.speaker: Duncan Weldon
insights.so_what: A historical benchmark suggesting integration is reversible and can peak, then unwind for decades, a caution against assuming globalisation is a one-way ratchet.
insights.quote: measures of global economic integration hit levels that would, in many cases, not be surpassed again until the 1980s
insights.locator: The word globalisation would not be coined

insights.claim: The transport revolution collapsed distance dramatically: Atlantic crossing time fell from about two weeks by steam in the mid-1840s to roughly a week by the 1880s, and world railway track grew from 125,000 miles in 1870 to over 620,000 miles by 1913.
insights.speaker: Duncan Weldon
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that a technology-driven fall in transaction costs, not policy alone, drove the first globalisation, a parallel to digital-era integration.
insights.locator: Take, as but one example, the time required to cross the Atlantic

insights.claim: Even strategic industries were cross-border by 1914: Berlin was almost as reliant on British coal as on Silesian coalfields, and six German factories in Russia produced 80 per cent of that nation's chemicals.
insights.speaker: Duncan Weldon
insights.so_what: Shows deep supply-chain entanglement failed to prevent war, a sobering data point for those citing chip or energy interdependence as a deterrent today.
insights.quote: six German factories in Russia were responsible for 80 per cent of the chemicals that nation produced
insights.locator: As Mulligan notes, even in strategic industries

insights.claim: Mulligan argues economic policy was increasingly weaponised for political ends: French governments directed capital toward Russian and Serbian military capacity while British planners studied using naval and financial power to destroy Germany's economy in a future war.
insights.speaker: Duncan Weldon
insights.so_what: The pre-1914 precedent for today's sanctions, financial statecraft and weaponised interdependence; the tools existed a century ago and helped drive escalation.
insights.quote: French governments directed capital flows towards building Russian and Serbian military capacity
insights.locator: What is more, economic and commercial policy

insights.claim: The 1911 Second Moroccan Crisis showed financial power as coercion: a flight of French capital pressured German markets and forced Berlin to back down, prompting Germany to expand its army to contain French power.
insights.speaker: Duncan Weldon
insights.so_what: A concrete case where a capital-flow shock translated into a military build-up, illustrating how financial coercion can escalate rather than resolve disputes.
insights.quote: a flight of French capital put pressure on Germany's own markets and forced Berlin to back down
insights.locator: Particularly after the Second Moroccan Crisis

insights.claim: Britain before 1914 faced the hegemon's dilemma, echoed by the modern United States: its role as lynchpin of the financial system both enriched it and let it harm foes, but exercising that power risked undermining the system underpinning its global role.
insights.speaker: Duncan Weldon
insights.so_what: A direct historical analogy for the dollar-weaponisation dilemma facing the US today: overusing financial hegemony can corrode its foundation.
insights.quote: Any exercising of such power risked undermining the whole world system that underpinned its global role.
insights.locator: Indeed, in an interesting parallel with the modern United States

themes.theme: Why peace lasted, and then broke

insights.claim: The reviewer suggests the more interesting question is why great-power peace lasted from 1871 to 1914, implying economic ties provided strong but ultimately insufficient incentives to avoid war through repeated crises.
insights.speaker: Duncan Weldon
insights.so_what: Reframes deterrence as a decades-long success that eventually failed, cautioning against reading long stretches of peace as permanent.
insights.quote: It may be that deepening economic ties were not enough to keep war at bay forever, but they at least provided strong incentives to avoid it for many decades
insights.locator: More generally, it can be argued

insights.claim: Mulligan's account holds that leaders in Germany, Italy, Austria-Hungary and Russia turned to military force to compensate for weaknesses in the economic sphere, driving an arms race and militarised diplomacy that left the old restraints wanting in the July Crisis.
insights.speaker: Duncan Weldon
insights.so_what: The mechanism to watch: economically weaker great powers substituting military assertiveness for economic strength, a pattern with contemporary resonance.
insights.quote: began to turn towards military force to compensate for weaknesses in the economic sphere
